doc.title: Paul Shaffer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 24, 2023

title: Learning records by ear and reproducing arrangements
summary: He learned pop songs by ear on piano, including orchestration lines like the oboe on Gene Pitney's 'Mecca'.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Did you start to notice arrangements, the particular sound of a record and what gave it some distinction from the person behind that we rarely hear about, the cat that arranged the horns and chose the — you know we’re going to put a harpsichord in here and all that. Did that seep into your consciousness?

I don’t think it did until much later. I was really, I mean I was hearing the records on the radio and zeroing in on them and certainly learning the arrangements because I was reproducing them on piano as a kid. Instead of practicing my piano lesson I’d start to hear these simple songs on the radio and find that I could play them all with just three and four chords just like a guitar-playing kid of today you know I learned those four chords and then I would also play the melody in my right hand, very simple but if I heard like an orchestration line for instance Gene Pitney I remember had a record that I loved called “Mecca” [sings] “I live on the West Side” and it had some oboe like a middle-eastern type of [scats] would come in and I would learn how to play that. And I’d really be reproducing the orchestration too. And that was kind of my, also what I did a lot of as a kid, and expanded my hearing and my hearing of chords that way. “Oh there’s a fifth chord. What’s that?” And it was as simple as that though, pretty easy to learn it step by step because the music was getting a little more sophisticated at a time. And then I guess really it wasn’t ‘til college when Blood, Sweat & Tears hit and they were very influential for me on the first album.
